analogy.p: Imagine a relay team: the pituitary hands the baton (FSH) to the ovary to prepare the runner (the egg); the ovary's oestrogen builds the track (uterus lining) and, when the track is ready, it shouts for the starting gun (LH surge) so the runner leaves at about day 14. Progesterone then keeps the track in good condition for any arrival. The contraceptive pill is like someone constantly shouting 'the race has already started' so the pituitary never sends the baton. The analogy breaks down because hormones act back on the pituitary through feedback, which a simple relay race does not have.
analogy.t: A relay race with a thermostat

bullets: **Reproductive hormones** cause **secondary sex characteristics** during puberty (exact spec wording).
**Testosterone** is the main male reproductive hormone, made in the **testes**.
**Oestrogen** is the main female reproductive hormone, made in the **ovaries**.
Puberty usually starts earlier in girls (about 8 to 13 years) than boys (about 9 to 14 years), but the timing varies a lot between people.
Primary sex characteristics are the sex organs present from birth (testes, ovaries); secondary ones develop at puberty.
Hormones are **chemical messengers** secreted by glands straight into the blood, so they act slowly but their effects last longer than nerve impulses.
Link to other topics: the pituitary is the 'master gland' because it makes hormones (FSH, LH) that control other glands.
core.p: **Puberty** is the stage of development when the body becomes able to reproduce. It is triggered by the brain and **pituitary gland**, which start releasing hormones that tell the **testes** (in boys) and **ovaries** (in girls) to start working. The gonads then secrete the main **reproductive hormones**, and these cause the **secondary sex characteristics**, the changes that distinguish adult males from adult females but are not the reproductive organs themselves. The hormones are carried in the **blood plasma** to their **target organs**, which is why this topic belongs with the endocrine system.

bullets: Made in the **testes**; carried in the blood; target organs include the testes themselves, muscle, skin and larynx.
**Stimulates sperm production** (spermatogenesis) in the testes.
Causes male secondary sex characteristics: facial and body hair, deepening voice (growth of the larynx), muscle development, wider shoulders, growth of the penis and testes.
Sperm are produced continuously from puberty, whereas females release about one egg per cycle.
The pituitary hormones FSH and LH stimulate the testes to make testosterone and sperm (extension beyond the spec).
Exam tip: do not say the prostate gland or the pituitary makes testosterone, it is the **testes**.
Testosterone is NOT the same as oestrogen: both sexes make small amounts of the other hormone, but each is the 'main' hormone of one sex only.
core.h: Testosterone and the male reproductive system
core.p: **Testosterone** is produced by the **testes** and is the main male reproductive hormone. At puberty its level rises sharply. It stimulates **sperm production** in the testes, which is the essential reproductive role the spec asks for, and it also causes the male secondary sex characteristics. Because it is a hormone it travels in the blood and affects many body tissues, not only the testes. From puberty onwards sperm are made continuously, unlike eggs in females, which are matured one at a time in a monthly cycle.

bullets: Made in the **ovaries**; stimulates the **maturation of an egg** (spec: 'one function is the maturation of an egg in the ovary').
Causes female secondary sex characteristics: breast development, growth of pubic and underarm hair, widening of the hips, and fat deposition.
Starts the **menstrual cycle** (periods) at puberty, which marks the ability to release eggs.
In the menstrual cycle oestrogen makes the **lining of the uterus grow** (thicken and develop a blood supply).
At high levels oestrogen stimulates the **LH surge** and inhibits FSH (Higher tier detail below).
The **ovary** contains many follicles from birth, each holding an immature egg, but usually only one matures in each cycle.
Do not confuse the **oviduct** (egg tube where fertilisation happens) with the **uterus** (womb where the embryo develops) or the **cervix** (ring of muscle at the bottom of the uterus).
core.h: Oestrogen and the female reproductive system
core.p: **Oestrogen** is the main female reproductive hormone and is produced by the **ovaries**. At puberty its level rises, and it causes the female secondary sex characteristics. Its key reproductive functions in the spec are the **maturation of an egg** in the ovary and, in the menstrual cycle, causing the **lining of the uterus to grow**. Oestrogen is made by the follicle (the fluid-filled sac in the ovary containing the developing egg), so a growing egg and a rising oestrogen level go together.

bullets: **Cycle length**: about 28 days (typical cycles range from about 21 to 35 days).
**Days 1 to about 5**: **menstruation**, the lining of the uterus is shed through the vagina as a period.
**Days about 5 to 14**: the lining **builds up again** and an egg matures in a follicle.
**Day 14 (about)**: **ovulation**, the egg is released from the ovary into the oviduct.
**Days 15 to 28**: the lining is **maintained**, ready for an embryo to implant.
If no fertilised egg arrives, hormone levels fall and the lining is shed again at day 1 of the next cycle.
The cycle is controlled by **four hormones**: FSH, LH, oestrogen and progesterone, two from the pituitary and two from the ovaries.
core.p: The **menstrual cycle** is a roughly **28 day** repeating sequence in females, from puberty until the menopause, in which an egg is matured and released and the uterus lining is prepared in case of pregnancy. **Day 1** is the first day of bleeding. **Ovulation**, the release of an egg from an ovary, happens at about **day 14**, half way through the cycle. If the egg is fertilised and the embryo implants, the lining must be kept; if not, the lining is shed and the cycle starts again. The cycle length varies from person to person and from month to month, so 28 days and day 14 are averages, which is why exam questions say 'about'.

bullets: **FSH** (follicle stimulating hormone), made in the **pituitary gland**: causes the **maturation of an egg** in the ovary (and stimulates the ovaries to produce oestrogen).
**LH** (luteinising hormone), made in the **pituitary gland**: **stimulates the release of the egg** (ovulation).
**Oestrogen**, made in the **ovaries**: causes the **lining of the uterus to grow** (and stimulates LH release; inhibits FSH, Higher tier).
**Progesterone**, made in the **ovaries** (by the empty follicle after ovulation): **maintains the lining of the uterus** (and inhibits FSH and LH, Higher tier).
Memory trick for the pituitary pair: **F**SH = **F**ollicle/egg matures; **L**H = **L**eaves (egg leaves the ovary).
Memory trick for the ovary pair: oestrogen = **grows** the lining; progesterone = **p**reserves/**p**rotects the lining for pregnancy.
The names include 'stimulating' because each hormone has a **target organ** that responds only to that hormone.
core.h: The four hormones: where they are made and what they do
core.p: Four hormones control the cycle and you must know each one's **source** and **function**. **FSH** and **LH** are made in the **pituitary gland** at the base of the brain; **oestrogen** and **progesterone** are made by the **ovaries**. The pituitary hormones act on the ovary, and the ovarian hormones act on the uterus and also feed back to the pituitary, which creates a control loop. Learn them as a table: hormone, made in, main job. Mark schemes want the exact job (matures egg, releases egg, grows lining, maintains lining), not vague words like 'helps the egg'.

bullets: **Days 1 to 5**: oestrogen and progesterone are low, so the thick lining cannot be maintained and is **shed**.
**Days 5 to 13**: **FSH** rises and an egg **matures** in a follicle; the follicle releases **oestrogen**, which **repairs and thickens** the lining.
**Around day 13**: oestrogen is at its peak, which stimulates a rapid rise in **LH** (the LH surge).
**Day 14**: **LH** causes **ovulation**; the egg enters the oviduct and can be fertilised for about a day.
**Days 15 to 28**: the empty follicle makes **progesterone**, which **maintains the lining** and also inhibits FSH and LH so another egg is not released.
**Day 28**: if the egg is not fertilised progesterone falls, the lining breaks down, and the next period begins.
If fertilisation occurs, the embryo implants in the thick lining, progesterone stays high and periods stop during pregnancy (this is why a missed period can be an early sign).
Why the lining matters: it provides a **blood supply** and nutrients to the embryo before the placenta forms.
core.h: Stage by stage through the cycle
core.p: Follow the cycle in order, naming the hormone at each stage and **why** it matters. In the first days the lining is shed because hormone levels are low. The pituitary then releases **FSH**, which causes a follicle to grow and an egg to mature while the follicle makes **oestrogen**. Oestrogen rebuilds the uterus lining. Around day 12 to 13 the oestrogen level is high enough to trigger a sudden **surge of LH**, and LH causes **ovulation** at about day 14. The empty follicle then secretes **progesterone**, which keeps the lining thick and blood-rich. If no embryo implants, progesterone falls, so the lining breaks down and menstruation begins.

bullets: **FSH stimulates oestrogen production** by the ovary (the follicle makes oestrogen as the egg matures).
**Oestrogen inhibits FSH** (negative feedback), so no more eggs than needed are matured.
**Oestrogen stimulates LH** release: the high oestrogen level at about day 13 causes the **LH surge** that triggers ovulation.
**Progesterone inhibits FSH and LH**, stopping more eggs maturing during the second half of the cycle.
When progesterone **falls** at the end of the cycle the inhibition is removed, FSH rises, and a new follicle starts to develop.
This control system is an example of **homeostasis-style feedback**, but unlike body temperature it produces a repeating cycle rather than a constant level.
This is exactly the principle used in the **combined contraceptive pill**: oestrogen and progesterone are taken to keep FSH low (see contraception).
In answers use the phrase 'inhibits the release of' rather than 'stops', and always name the hormone and its source.
core.p: At Higher tier you must explain how the hormones **interact**, not just list them. The key idea is **negative feedback**: a rise in one hormone switches off the release of another. Early in the cycle FSH causes the ovary to make **oestrogen**. Oestrogen then **inhibits FSH** so only one dominant egg matures. When oestrogen has risen high enough it also **stimulates the pituitary to release a surge of LH**, which is a positive effect at the cycle's mid-point. After ovulation **progesterone** inhibits both FSH and LH, which prevents another egg maturing while the lining is maintained. When the follicle degenerates, progesterone falls, the inhibition is lifted, FSH rises and the cycle restarts.

bullets: Read the axes: x axis = **day of cycle** (0 to 28), y axis = hormone level in arbitrary units or concentration.
**Ovulation** is found at the day of the **LH peak** (or just after it, about day 14).
**Oestrogen** rises through days 5 to 13, falls after ovulation and has a smaller second rise in the second half.
**Progesterone** is near zero until ovulation, rises to a peak at about day 21, then falls before the period.
When progesterone is high the lining is **thick**; when it falls the lining is shed.
Calculate **percentage change** = (change in value ÷ original value) × 100; always show the subtraction.
To describe a trend: say what the line does, over which days, and give two values from the graph with units.
To explain: link the shape to the hormone's job, e.g. 'LH peaks at day 13 because it stimulates release of the egg'.
Common trap: reading the wrong line or the wrong axis (use a ruler and the key).
core.p: Exam questions often give a graph of hormone levels against day of the cycle. Treat it as a skill with a method. First identify each line using the key. Then link features of the graph to events: the **LH peak** (surge) occurs just before **ovulation** (day 14); the **oestrogen peak** comes slightly before the LH peak; **progesterone** is low in the first half and high in the second half; **FSH** is high early and has a small peak at mid cycle. Use data from the graph in your answer (quote days and values) and state a **trend** before explaining it using the hormone's function.

bullets: Three stages that can be blocked: (1) egg maturation and release, (2) sperm reaching the egg, (3) implantation of an embryo.
**Hormonal methods** are only used by females and mainly block stage 1 (and some thicken mucus for stage 2).
**Non-hormonal methods** include barrier methods, IUDs, spermicides, abstaining and sterilisation.
Effectiveness depends on **correct use**: a method that is highly effective in theory can fail in real life if forgotten (pill) or used wrongly (condom).
Only **condoms** (male or female) protect against **sexually transmitted infections** (STIs); hormonal methods do not.
Contraception allows people to plan the number and spacing of children, which has health, social and economic effects.
Choosing a method involves personal, medical and sometimes **religious or ethical** factors.
core.p: **Contraception** means methods that reduce the chance of pregnancy. Pregnancy needs an egg to be **released**, sperm to **reach and fertilise** the egg, and the embryo to **implant** in the uterus lining. Every method works by blocking at least one of these three stages. The spec divides them into **hormonal** methods, which change the female's hormone levels, and **non-hormonal** methods, which act physically, chemically or surgically. Being able to say which stage a method blocks, and to compare methods, is the heart of the exam questions on this topic.

bullets: **Oral contraceptive**: contains oestrogen and progesterone; **inhibits FSH** so eggs do not mature.
**Progesterone** also causes **thick cervical mucus**, blocking sperm.
**Injection, implant or skin patch**: slow release of progesterone, inhibiting egg maturation and release for **months or years**.
**Advantages**: very effective when used correctly, reversible, do not interrupt sex, and the implant and injection do not need daily action.
**Disadvantages**: can cause **side effects** (headaches, nausea, mood changes, irregular bleeding, raised blood pressure or small clot risk with some pills).
**Disadvantages**: the pill must be taken every day at about the same time, so it can fail if doses are missed or vomiting occurs.
**No protection against STIs**, so condoms may still be advised.
Link to the cycle: the pill gives constant hormone levels that mimic the post-ovulation phase, so the pituitary 'thinks' ovulation has happened.
core.p: **Oral contraceptives** (the pill) contain **oestrogen and progesterone**. These hormones **inhibit the production of FSH**, so no eggs mature in the ovary and ovulation does not occur. Progesterone also stimulates the production of **thick cervical mucus**, which prevents the passage of sperm into the uterus. Other hormonal methods deliver **slow-release progesterone** over a long period: a contraceptive **injection**, a small **implant** under the skin, or a **skin patch**. These inhibit the maturation and release of eggs for **months or even years**. Because they use the body's own feedback system (progesterone and oestrogen suppress FSH and LH), they link directly to the Higher tier content above.

bullets: **Condom** (male or female): barrier stopping sperm reaching the egg; also gives **protection against STIs**.
**Diaphragm**: a rubber cap fitted over the cervix that blocks sperm; more effective when used with a spermicide.
**IUD**: prevents implantation of an embryo; some types release a **hormone** (progesterone), others use copper; long-lasting and reversible.
**Spermicidal agent**: chemical that kills or disables sperm; less effective alone.
**Abstaining**: no intercourse when an egg may be in the oviduct; unreliable because cycles vary.
**Female sterilisation**: the oviducts are cut or tied so the egg cannot meet sperm.
**Male sterilisation**: the sperm ducts are cut or tied (vasectomy) so sperm are not in semen.
Sterilisation is usually **permanent** and is chosen by people who do not want more children.
core.p: Non-hormonal methods do not change the hormones. **Barrier methods** such as **condoms** and **diaphragms** physically **prevent the sperm reaching the egg**. **Intrauterine devices (IUDs)** are placed in the uterus and **prevent the implantation of an embryo** (and some also **release a hormone**). **Spermicidal agents** (creams, foams or gels) **kill or disable sperm**. **Abstaining from intercourse** when an egg may be in the oviduct (around ovulation) avoids pregnancy but needs accurate prediction of the fertile time. **Surgical methods** of male and female **sterilisation** are very effective but usually permanent.

bullets: **Most effective** in typical use: long-acting methods that need no daily action (implant, IUD, sterilisation).
**Condoms** are the only method that also prevents STIs; they are effective if used correctly every time.
**The pill** is very effective when taken correctly, but human error makes it less effective in practice.
**Reversibility**: pill, injection, implant, IUD and barrier methods are reversible; sterilisation is normally not.
**Side effects** only apply to hormonal methods (and the copper IUD can cause heavier periods).
**Ethical and religious views**: some religions and individuals object to artificial contraception; others see it as responsible family planning.
**Social factors**: availability, cost (many are free on the NHS), age and consent.
In 6 mark answers use a table-style structure in prose: 'Method A is ... because ...; however ...; method B ...; overall ...'.
core.p: Exam questions ask you to **evaluate** or **compare** methods. Use a fixed set of criteria: **effectiveness** (how likely to prevent pregnancy, including real-life use), **side effects and health risks**, **protection against STIs**, **reversibility** (can the person try for a baby later), **convenience** (daily action or one-off), and **personal or religious beliefs**. A good answer states a point for each method and finishes with a justified conclusion linked to the person's circumstances rather than just saying 'it is best'.

bullets: Link: **IVF** uses FSH and LH to stimulate eggs to mature, the same hormones in the menstrual cycle.
Link: **fertility drugs** work by supplying what the body lacks, while the **pill** works by suppressing FSH.
Link: **negative feedback** also controls blood glucose (insulin/glucagon) and water (ADH).
Link: **pituitary** hormones (FSH, LH, ADH, growth hormone) all act on target organs through the blood.
Link: **STIs** such as chlamydia and HIV; only condoms prevent transmission (communicable disease topic).
Link: **puberty** hormones also explain adolescent changes in behaviour and growth.
Synoptic skill: state the structure involved (e.g. oviduct), the hormone and the effect, in that order.
Quality of written communication on 6 mark questions rewards logical sequence: cause then effect then outcome.
core.h: Links to other topics and exam synthesis
core.p: This topic links to many others, which is why it often appears as a synoptic question. The cycle is regulated by **negative feedback**, like blood glucose and body temperature, but it produces a repeating pattern. The pituitary shows how one gland controls another (**endocrine system**). Contraception connects to **STIs** (communicable disease), to **IVF** and infertility treatment (hormones used to boost fertility), and to **ethics** when you weigh up benefits and risks. When asked to 'explain', name the hormone, its source and its target and describe the effect; when asked to 'evaluate', give both sides and a judgement.

exam: 'State/Name' (1 mark): give the hormone and its source, e.g. 'FSH from the pituitary gland'.
'Describe the role of' (2 marks): hormone + function, e.g. 'LH stimulates the release of the egg (ovulation)'.
Menstrual cycle questions: always use the day numbers (1 to 5, 14, 28) and name which hormone is acting at each stage.
6 mark 'Explain how the hormones control the cycle': structure it chronologically: FSH, oestrogen, LH surge, ovulation, progesterone, fall in progesterone and period.
Higher tier: always name the feedback, e.g. 'oestrogen inhibits FSH' and 'high oestrogen stimulates LH release'.
Graph questions: identify the line from the key, quote values and days from the graph, then explain with the hormone's function.
Percentage change: (new minus old) divided by old, times 100; show working for the mark.
'Explain how the pill prevents pregnancy' (3 to 4 marks): oestrogen and progesterone, inhibit FSH, no egg matures, thick mucus blocks sperm.
'Evaluate' contraception (4 to 6 marks): give an advantage and disadvantage for each method (effectiveness, side effects, STIs, reversibility) then a conclusion.
Command word 'suggest': apply knowledge to an unfamiliar situation, e.g. why a missed pill may cause pregnancy (FSH no longer inhibited).
Spelling: oestrogen, progesterone, ovulation, uterus, oviduct; wrong terms such as 'womb tube' are not credited.

mistakes.r: FSH causes the maturation of an egg; LH stimulates its release (ovulation).
Menstruation is days 1 to about 5; ovulation is at about day 14.
mistakes.w: The period happens at ovulation / day 14.

mistakes.r: Progesterone (and oestrogen) are made by the ovaries; FSH and LH are made by the pituitary.
mistakes.w: Progesterone is made by the pituitary gland.

mistakes.r: Testosterone is produced by the testes and stimulates sperm production.
mistakes.w: Testosterone is made by the prostate gland or the pituitary.

mistakes.r: The pill inhibits FSH so no eggs mature (and progesterone thickens cervical mucus so sperm cannot pass).
No method is 100% effective; only condoms give protection against STIs, the pill does not.
mistakes.w: Condoms are 100% effective and the pill protects against STIs.

mistakes.r: An IUD prevents the implantation of an embryo (some also release a hormone).
mistakes.w: An IUD stops the egg being released.

mistakes.r: Oestrogen causes the lining to grow; progesterone maintains it.
Ovulation is the release of an egg; fertilisation occurs only if sperm meet the egg in the oviduct.

summary: The spec asks you to know how reproductive hormones cause puberty and secondary sex characteristics, how FSH, LH, oestrogen and progesterone (with their sources) control the 28 day menstrual cycle and ovulation, how these hormones interact (Higher tier), and how hormonal and non-hormonal contraception work and can be evaluated. It matters because it is a regular source of 6 mark 'explain' questions, graph interpretation and evaluation of social and ethical choices.

The control chain: the pituitary releases FSH and LH, the ovaries release oestrogen and progesterone, and these feed back to the pituitary (negative feedback).

terms.d: The stage of development when reproductive hormones cause secondary sex characteristics and the body becomes capable of reproduction.
Changes at puberty caused by reproductive hormones that distinguish adult males and females (e.g. body hair, voice change, breast development).
The main male reproductive hormone, produced by the testes; stimulates sperm production.
The main female reproductive hormone, produced by the ovaries; involved in maturation of an egg and growth of the uterus lining.
A cycle of about 28 days in which an egg matures and is released and the uterus lining grows and is maintained or shed.
The release of a mature egg from an ovary, at about day 14 of the cycle.
Pituitary hormone that causes the maturation of an egg in the ovary and stimulates oestrogen production.
Pituitary hormone that stimulates the release of an egg (ovulation).
Hormone produced by the ovaries (empty follicle) that maintains the lining of the uterus.
The master gland at the base of the brain that secretes FSH, LH and other hormones.
A change in one hormone causes an effect that reduces or inhibits that change or another hormone, e.g. oestrogen inhibits FSH.
A pill containing oestrogen and progesterone that inhibits FSH production so that no eggs mature.
A contraceptive that physically stops sperm reaching an egg, such as a condom or diaphragm.
A device placed in the uterus that prevents implantation of an embryo and may release a hormone.
A chemical that kills or disables sperm.
A surgical method of contraception in which the oviducts (female) or sperm ducts (male) are cut or tied.
The organ or tissue that responds to a particular hormone.

worked.q:
The table shows hormone levels (arbitrary units) at selected days of a menstrual cycle.
Day: 1, 5, 9, 12, 13, 14, 21, 28
LH: 3, 3, 4, 8, 38, 12, 4, 3
Oestrogen: 40, 50, 120, 220, 200, 100, 180, 40
(a) On which day was an egg most likely released? (1)
(b) Calculate the percentage increase in oestrogen from day 5 to day 12. (2)
(c) Explain why the uterus lining is not shed between days 14 and 28. (2)
steps: (a) The LH surge triggers ovulation, and LH is highest at day 13 (38 units); ovulation follows at about day 14.
(c) After ovulation the empty follicle secretes progesterone.
Progesterone maintains the lining, so it is not shed until progesterone levels fall at about day 28.

worked.ans: Model answer: The pill contains oestrogen and progesterone, which inhibit FSH production so that eggs do not mature or get released. Progesterone also makes the cervical mucus thick so sperm cannot pass through.
worked.q: Explain how the combined contraceptive pill prevents pregnancy. (4 marks)
steps: The pill contains oestrogen and progesterone (1).
These hormones inhibit the production of FSH by the pituitary gland (1).
With low FSH, no egg matures in the ovary, so no egg is released (1).
Progesterone also thickens cervical mucus, which prevents sperm passing into the uterus (1).

worked.ans: Model answer: Condoms stop sperm reaching the egg and are the only method that also protects against STIs, but they can fail if used incorrectly. The implant releases progesterone slowly, inhibiting the maturation and release of eggs for years, so it is very effective and needs no daily action, though it may have side effects and gives no STI protection. Overall the implant is more effective at preventing pregnancy, but condoms are the better choice if STI protection matters, so using both gives the best protection.
worked.q: A couple want to avoid pregnancy. Evaluate the use of condoms compared with the contraceptive implant. (6 marks)
steps: Condom: a barrier method that physically stops sperm reaching the egg (1).
Advantage: protects against STIs, no hormonal side effects, easily available (1).
Disadvantage: relies on correct use every time; can split or be put on wrongly so less effective in real life (1).
Implant: slow release of progesterone inhibits egg maturation and release for years (1).
Advantage: very effective as no daily action needed, reversible; disadvantage: no STI protection and may cause side effects such as irregular bleeding (1).
Conclusion: implant is better for pregnancy prevention long term but condoms are needed for STI protection, so using both may be best (1).
